content:
Lean core defines what a SAT-problem is in Std.Sat. As far as I can see, this formalization works with arrays now (which some months ago was not the case).
For the formalization of Cook-Levin, I want to work with SAT-instances and need to write down some explicitly. Is Std.Sat the right tool to work with for this, or does CSLib have some other implementation of what a SAT-instance is (i.e. a "more abstract" / mathsy one)?

I'd be happy to receive some feedback on how CSLib would want to approach this.

We do not generally define SAT problems, the machinery there only covers CNFs and AIGs, implemented (somewhat, the CNF still needs improvements) efficiently for decision procedure purposes. There is a general notion of boolean expressions with a connection to the CNFs available but this is not meant as a publicly facing API.
Note that at some undetermined point in the future the definition of a clause is going to change so I would advise to build/use API around its concrete datastructures if you decide to go with it
Specifically CNFs is all I need, so working with Std.Sat is fine for me. I just wanted to check whether CSLib has its own (preferred) version to handle SATs

This is fairly trivial. My EFX formalisation had a single file for defining SAT formulas and their satisfiability. Denote by ι\iotaι an index type of variables. Define literals as Pos or Neg elements of this type. Then clauses are just lists of literals and CNFs and DNFs are lists of clauses. An assignment is a function ι↦Bool\iota \mapsto \texttt{Bool}ι↦Bool and you can define satisfaction and validity with respect to such assignments.
I can upstream it if you like. I just don’t see much use for it in CSLib. You might want to check on the propositional logic thread.

I've been working on formalizing DPLL, and @Shreyas Srinivas 's representation of CNFs is the same as what I settled on. So IMO we should go with that. We're still sorting out the syntax and semantics of propositional logic, but for Cook-Levin, all you need is CNF machinery, as you said. Maybe make a PR with just that?

While I agree with you/shreyas on how to represent a CNF, this is not what my question was about.
The existing Std.Sat file already models CNF as exactly that (up to wrapping it in a structure).
My question was whether CSLib would want to use that file, or prefers (possibly existing) their own version of what a SAT is.
So, I don't see the value of making a PR with just CNFs (because it already exists as Std.Sat), unless there is specific other design goals that CSLib wants to fulfill (but I wouldn't know about).
Hence, at least for now, just using Std.Sat seems to be the correct choice, no?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. I kind of prefer having an inductive type with Pos and Neg over the way Std.Sat does it with abbrev Literal (α : Type u) := α × Bool, but probably better not to reinvent the wheel here.
Okay, thanks for the recommendations :thumbs_up:

Matthew Doty said:

Yeah, I think that makes sense. I kind of prefer having an inductive type with Pos and Neg over the way Std.Sat does it with abbrev Literal (α : Type u) := α × Bool, but probably better not to reinvent the wheel here.

For the record, we will change exactly this part about Std.Sat in the future so whatever development is made on top of Std.Sat should not extensively rely on this fact but try to abstract over it.
